approved: Migration and Maritime Powers Legislation Amendment (Resolving the Asylum Legacy Caseload) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change how Australia handles people smuggling and asylum seekers both at sea and on land.
It would give the government stronger maritime enforcement powers, create temporary protection visas, and set up a fast-track assessment process for certain asylum claims.
The bill would let the minister cap the number of protection visas granted each year and remove the 90-day deadline for deciding such visas.
Reinforces maritime enforcement powers to stop people smuggling ventures at sea.
Introduces Temporary Protection Visas and Safe Haven Enterprise Visas for unauthorised arrivals who qualify for protection.
Creates a fast-track assessment process that bypasses the Refugee Review Tribunal for some applicants.
Codifies Australia's interpretation of its refugee obligations under the Refugees Convention into the Migration Act.
Retrospectively clarifies that children born to unauthorised maritime arrivals or transitory persons are also treated as such.
Restores the government's ability to set a statutory limit on protection visas granted per year and removes the 90-day decision requirement.

Asylum seekers who arrive illegally in Australia, including unauthorised maritime arrivals and transitory persons, as well as government officers and agencies involved in maritime operations and protection assessments.

Moved a bill to resolve Labor's legacy caseload of around 30,000 asylum claims, reintroducing temporary protection visas valid for up to three years and creating a new five-year Safe Haven Enterprise Visa for regional work, under which holders who work without income support for 3.5 years can apply for other onshore visas, and established a fast-track assessment process with a new Immigration Assessment Authority to replace merits review for unmeritorious claims.

Announced Labor will oppose the Migration and Maritime Powers Legislation Amendment bill in the House, objecting to a schedule that would render redundant a pending High Court case on turning back asylum boats, opposing the reintroduction of temporary protection visas, and citing government figures showing only 14 per cent of protection visa decisions now meet the 90-day rule, down from about half under Labor.
Argued that Labor is hypocritical in claiming the humanitarian high ground on asylum seeker policy, despite the outcomes of its own border protection record while in government.

Spoke in support of the bill, arguing that it would stop boat arrivals, address a 30,000-person legacy caseload, strengthen maritime enforcement, introduce temporary protection and safe haven enterprise visas, and support regional communities through work and study.
